module_intro: Treats the imbalance left behind by displacement in depth: FVG formation, FVGs created by displacement (quality grading), FVG as a PD array, Consequent Encroachment (CE), FVG retracement/continuation/failure, FVG relative to the dealing range and to liquidity, multiple/nested FVGs, HTF vs LTF FVGs, and a selection checklist.
prerequisites_stated_in_text: Requires Beginner Module 5 (Displacement & Imbalance) and Intermediate Modules 1-3.
module_objectives: Identify a Fair Value Gap (FVG) using the standard three-candle formation.
Recognise that high-quality FVGs are typically created by displacement.
Treat the FVG as a PD array and locate its Consequent Encroachment (50 % midpoint).
Distinguish FVG retracement (entry) behaviour from FVG continuation or failure.
Evaluate an FVG relative to the dealing range (premium/discount) and relative to liquidity.
Select among multiple or nested FVGs using context rather than treating every gap as equal.
Differentiate higher-timeframe FVGs (context) from lower-timeframe FVGs (execution).
Recognise when an FVG has failed or been fully mitigated and should no longer be used as support/resistance in its original direction.

concepts.name: Fair Value Gap Formation
concepts.definition:
A Fair Value Gap is a three-candle imbalance:
- Bullish FVG: the low of candle 3 is higher than the high of candle 1, leaving an unfilled space (the gap) across the body of candle 2.
- Bearish FVG: the high of candle 3 is lower than the low of candle 1, leaving an unfilled space across the body of candle 2.
- The gap represents a region where one-sided order flow was so dominant that two-sided delivery did not occur.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:

- The gap represents a region where one-sided order flow was so dominant that two-sided delivery did not occur.

raw_sections.Standard Definition:
A Fair Value Gap is a three-candle imbalance:

600. Bullish FVG: the low of candle 3 is higher than the high of candle 1, leaving an unfilled space (the gap) across the body of candle 2.

601. Bearish FVG: the high of candle 3 is lower than the low of candle 1, leaving an unfilled space across the body of candle 2.

The gap represents a region where one-sided order flow was so dominant that two-sided delivery did not occur.
raw_sections.Visual Check: If the wick of candle 1 and the wick of candle 3 overlap or touch, no standard FVG exists. Only a clear separation qualifies.

raw_sections.Preferred Origin: The highest-quality FVGs are those left by the displacement leg that also produced a Market Structure Shift (Module 3). These gaps sit inside a confirmed change of structural control and are therefore more reliable as later entry arrays.
raw_sections.Lower-Quality Gaps: Gaps that form inside tight, overlapping ranges or without preceding liquidity events and displacement are lower priority. They may still be mitigated, but they do not carry the same narrative weight.

concepts.name: Fair Value Gap as a PD Array

raw_sections.Role: Within the ICT framework a Fair Value Gap functions as a Premium/Discount Array - a price level or zone where the algorithm is expected to show interest on a return visit. Bullish FVGs are potential support (buy-side arrays); bearish FVGs are potential resistance (sell-side arrays).
raw_sections.Hierarchy Note: An FVG does not automatically outrank every other PD array. Its relative strength depends on the timeframe on which it formed, whether it remains unmitigated, its location inside the dealing range, and confluence with liquidity and structure.

concepts.name: Consequent Encroachment
concepts.definition: Consequent Encroachment (CE) is the 50 % midpoint of the Fair Value Gap (or of any measured PD array). It is also referred to as the mean threshold of the gap.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: Consequent Encroachment (CE) is the 50 % midpoint of the Fair Value Gap (or of any measured PD array). It is also referred to as the mean threshold of the gap.

raw_sections.Definition: Consequent Encroachment (CE) is the 50 % midpoint of the Fair Value Gap (or of any measured PD array). It is also referred to as the mean threshold of the gap.
raw_sections.Practical Importance: Price frequently reacts at or near the CE rather than requiring a full fill of the entire gap. Intermediate practice therefore often uses the CE as a refined entry reference or as a decision point inside the larger FVG zone.
raw_sections.How to Locate:
- Identify the upper and lower boundaries of the FVG.

- Calculate or draw the exact halfway point between those boundaries.

- Mark that level as Consequent Encroachment.
raw_sections.Usage: Common intermediate applications include placing a limit order at CE, requiring price to reach at least CE before considering the gap "tested," or using a close through CE as part of a mitigation/failure reading.

raw_sections.Retracement (Entry Context): After displacement creates an FVG and structure has shifted, price often retraces into the gap. A reaction from the gap (or from its CE) that resumes the direction of the displacement is the classic FVG continuation entry.
raw_sections.Continuation Through the Gap: If price enters the FVG and continues through it without meaningful rejection, the gap is being mitigated and may lose its original supportive or resistive character.
raw_sections.FVG Failure: An FVG fails in its original role when price closes decisively through the far side of the gap (beyond the boundary opposite the direction of the original displacement) and subsequently treats the zone from the opposite side. A fully mitigated bullish FVG can later act as resistance (and vice versa); this is sometimes discussed in community material as an inversion or inverted FVG, but the core ICT observation is simply that the original imbalance has been filled and the array's polarity may reverse.

concepts.name: FVG Relative to the Dealing Range

raw_sections.Premium / Discount Filter: A bullish FVG that sits in discount (below dealing-range equilibrium) is higher quality for long entries than the same FVG located in premium. A bearish FVG in premium is higher quality for short entries than one located in discount.
raw_sections.Practical Rule: When multiple FVGs exist, prefer the one that is both unmitigated and located in the correct half of the dealing range relative to the intended trade direction.

book_location.section_heading: FVG Relative to the Dealing Range

raw_sections.Ideal Sequence: The preferred intermediate sequence remains: liquidity event -> displacement (creating the FVG) -> Market Structure Shift -> retracement into the FVG. An FVG that forms after a clear liquidity raid and structural shift is more actionable than an isolated gap with no liquidity context.
raw_sections.Targeting: Once price reacts from an FVG, the logical targets are the Draw on Liquidity objectives established in Module 2 (internal then external, or external then internal, according to the narrative).

raw_sections.Multiple FVGs:
A single displacement leg can leave more than one FVG. Selection priority generally favours:

602. The FVG that overlaps Consequent Encroachment of a larger structure or an Order Block.

603. The FVG that sits deepest in the correct premium/discount half.

604. The most recent unmitigated FVG created by the displacement that produced the MSS.
raw_sections.Nested FVGs: A lower-timeframe FVG that forms inside a higher-timeframe FVG creates nested imbalance. This is a high-confluence location: the larger gap supplies context; the smaller gap supplies precision.

raw_sections.Roles:
Higher-timeframe FVGs (daily, 4-hour) act as contextual PD arrays and Draw-on-Liquidity magnets. They help define bias and the larger dealing-range narrative.

Lower-timeframe FVGs (15-minute, 5-minute, 1-minute) act as execution arrays. They refine the precise entry after a lower-timeframe MSS has confirmed inside the higher-timeframe zone.
raw_sections.Alignment: The highest-probability intermediate setups occur when a lower-timeframe FVG forms inside (or at the edge of) a higher-timeframe FVG or other HTF PD array, after a liquidity event and displacement on the lower timeframe.

rules.statement: FVG standard definition (three-candle imbalance): Bullish FVG -- the low of candle 3 is higher than the high of candle 1, leaving an unfilled space (the gap) across the body of candle 2. Bearish FVG is the mirror. Visual check: if the wick of candle 1 and the wick of candle 3 overlap or touch, no standard FVG exists -- only a clear separation qualifies.

Consequent Encroachment (CE) is the 50% midpoint of the Fair Value Gap (or of any measured PD array), also called the mean threshold of the gap. Located by: identifying the upper/lower boundaries of the FVG, calculating the exact halfway point, and marking that level as CE. Price frequently reacts at or near the CE rather than requiring a full fill of the entire gap; common intermediate applications include placing a limit order at CE, requiring price to reach at least CE before considering the gap 'tested,' or using a close through CE as part of a mitigation/failure reading.

An FVG fails in its original role when price closes decisively through the far side of the gap (beyond the boundary opposite the direction of the original displacement) and subsequently treats the zone from the opposite side. A fully mitigated bullish FVG can later act as resistance (and vice versa) -- the array's polarity may reverse once the original imbalance is filled.

A bullish FVG sitting in discount (below dealing-range equilibrium) is higher quality for long entries than the same FVG located in premium; a bearish FVG in premium is higher quality for short entries than one in discount. When multiple FVGs exist, prefer the one that is both unmitigated and located in the correct half of the dealing range relative to the intended trade direction.

rules.statement: Multiple FVG selection priority (when a single displacement leg leaves more than one FVG): (1) the FVG that overlaps Consequent Encroachment of a larger structure or an Order Block; (2) the FVG that sits deepest in the correct premium/discount half; (3) the most recent unmitigated FVG created by the displacement that produced the MSS. Nested FVGs (a lower-timeframe FVG forming inside a higher-timeframe FVG) create a high-confluence location: the larger gap supplies context, the smaller gap supplies precision.

FVG Selection Checklist (before treating an FVG as a high-quality entry array, ask): Was the FVG created by clear displacement (preferably after a liquidity event)? Does a Market Structure Shift accompany or immediately follow the displacement? Is the FVG still unmitigated (or only partially mitigated)? Does the FVG sit in the correct half of the dealing range for the intended direction? Is there confluence with another PD array, Consequent Encroachment of a larger structure, or a liquidity pool? Is the FVG on the appropriate timeframe for the role it is being asked to play (context vs execution)? If several answers are negative, the gap is lower priority or should be ignored.

examples.content:
Context: 1-hour dealing range 1.2500 - 1.2700, equilibrium 1.2600. Daily bias bullish. Price has just raided sell-side liquidity near 1.2520 and displaced higher, breaking a short-term high and leaving a clear bullish FVG between 1.2540 and 1.2565. Consequent Encroachment sits at approximately 1.2552.

Assessment:

605. Displacement after liquidity: yes.

606. MSS present: yes (internal).

607. Location: discount relative to the 1-hour range: yes.

608. Unmitigated: yes.

Execution focus: wait for a retracement into the FVG, with preference for a reaction at or near CE (1.2552). Stop conceptually beyond the origin of the displacement or the far side of the gap. Targets: internal buy-side liquidity first, then external objectives consistent with the daily Draw on Liquidity.

relationships.statement:
Displacement (Module 3) creates the FVG. The FVG becomes a PD array whose Consequent Encroachment refines the entry. Location inside the dealing range (Module 1) and relationship to liquidity (Module 2) filter which gaps are worth trading. Higher-timeframe gaps supply context; lower-timeframe gaps supply timing. Failure or full mitigation removes the gap from the list of active arrays in its original polarity.

Module 5 will place Order Blocks, Breakers and Mitigation Blocks alongside the FVG so that the full PD-array toolkit can be ranked and combined.

contradictions_or_ambiguities.description: The book distinguishes between the 'core ICT observation' (a fully mitigated FVG's polarity may reverse) and community terminology that labels this phenomenon an 'inversion' or 'inverted FVG (IFVG)' -- flagging the specific IFVG naming as community-originated rather than confirmed core ICT doctrine.

passage_a.text: A fully mitigated bullish FVG can later act as resistance (and vice versa); this is sometimes discussed in community material as an inversion or inverted FVG, but the core ICT observation is simply that the original imbalance has been filled and the array's polarity may reverse.

passage_b.text: unspecified - no directly conflicting passage; flagged as a naming/attribution distinction rather than a factual contradiction.

key_terms: Fair Value Gap (FVG) - three-candle imbalance left by one-sided delivery.
Bullish FVG - gap between candle-1 high and candle-3 low; potential support.
Bearish FVG - gap between candle-1 low and candle-3 high; potential resistance.
Consequent Encroachment (CE) - 50 % midpoint of the FVG (mean threshold).
Mitigation - price trading through the gap, filling the imbalance.
FVG failure / inversion - original polarity lost after decisive close through the far side.
Nested FVG - lower-timeframe gap forming inside a higher-timeframe gap.
PD array - price-delivery array; the FVG is one member of the set.
module_review_notes.beginner_summary: Beginner teaching introduced the FVG as an imbalance that price may return to. Intermediate teaching adds Consequent Encroachment, the requirement that high-quality gaps arise from displacement after liquidity and MSS, premium/discount location filters, multi-timeframe roles, and explicit failure conditions.
module_review_notes.concept_relationships_summary: Liquidity event + displacement (Modules 2 - 3) create the FVG. Dealing-range location (Module 1) filters it. CE refines the entry. Nested and multi-timeframe relationships supply confluence. Failure removes it from active consideration in the original direction.
module_review_notes.practical_chart_exercise:
On a liquid instrument:

- Mark every visible FVG on the 15-minute chart within the last two sessions.

- For each, note whether it was created by clear displacement and whether an MSS accompanied it.

- Locate Consequent Encroachment of the two highest-quality gaps.

- Classify each gap as sitting in premium or discount relative to the active 1-hour dealing range.

- Identify any nested relationship with a 1-hour or 4-hour FVG.

- Record which gaps were later respected, which were mitigated, and which failed, and write a one-sentence lesson from each outcome.

common_misconceptions: "Every FVG will be respected." - False. Context, location and mitigation status matter.
"I must wait for a full fill of the gap." - Not required; CE is often sufficient.
"An FVG on any timeframe is equally important." - False. HTF gaps are contextual; LTF gaps are for timing.
"Once price touches the gap the trade is confirmed." - False. Reaction quality and higher-timeframe alignment still govern.
"A mitigated FVG can never be useful again." - Overstated; a fully mitigated gap may later act from the opposite side, but that is a different (inverted) reading.
